strengths: Compelling mechanistic-to-intervention bridge: The paper translates recent mechanistic insights on emergent misalignment (specifically causal SAE persona features) into an effective, training-time regularization technique (BLOCK-EM).

Principled and simple formulation: The base-anchored, one-sided directional latent penalty is intuitive, computationally feasible, and directly penalizes movement only in the harmful directions without constraining orthogonal model adaptation.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across six distinct downstream domains (Finance, Health, Legal, Career, Edu, PrimeVul) and three model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen-2.5-7B), consistently demonstrating significant reductions in emergent misalignment (~90–95%) while maintaining high in-domain task adherence and output coherence.

Methodological rigor and ablations: The evaluation carefully maintains disjoint sets for latent discovery versus final evaluation. Extensive ablations validate key components, demonstrating that causal screening beats simple correlation/top-delta, signed directionality is essential, and random latent penalties do not work.

Honest and insightful characterization of failure modes: Section 5 provides an exemplary scientific investigation into misalignment re-emergence under multi-epoch fine-tuning, using downstream freezing, activation patching, and residual steering capacity to localize rerouting to upstream layers (hypothesis H2).
weaknesses: Small evaluation prompt suites: The evaluation relies on a relatively compact set of benchmark prompts (44 core discovery prompts and 29 held-out evaluation prompts). While following existing literature (e.g., Wang et al., 2025; Betley et al., 2025), a larger and broader benchmark suite would provide higher statistical power and narrower confidence intervals.

Dependence on a diagnostic misaligned model: The feature discovery pipeline requires an initial misaligned checkpoint $M_{\text{mis}}$ to perform model-diffing. Although the paper shows that latents transfer across domains (allowing practitioners to reuse pre-extracted latents), discovering new latent sets for novel architectures or behaviors requires an initial fine-tuning run to elicit misalignment.

Vulnerability to prolonged optimization pressure: As demonstrated in Section 5, single-layer latent blocking is circumvented under prolonged multi-epoch training via alternative representational pathways, showing that fixed single-layer constraints are not fully robust against persistent gradient pressure.

strengths: Compelling connection between mechanistic interpretability and training-time alignment: The paper bridges Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature discovery and causal steering with a practical training regularizer (BLOCK-EM), moving beyond passive analysis or inference-time steering to representation-guided fine-tuning.

Methodological rigor and experimental hygiene: The authors carefully enforce disjoint prompt splits for feature discovery (core misalignment) versus benchmark evaluation (final evaluation), use multiple independent 70B+ LLM judges, report multi-seed results with standard error bars, and track generation quality (incoherence, refusal) alongside in-domain adherence.

Comprehensive baselines and mechanistic ablations: BLOCK-EM demonstrates a superior safety-utility trade-off compared to competitive baselines including KL-divergence penalties, inoculation prompting, preventative steering, and post-hoc test-time steering. Extensive ablations (random latents, Top-Delta, sign shuffling, and latent set size sweeps) validate the causal specificity of the identified latents.

Impressive cross-domain transfer and model generality: Causal latents discovered in a single domain (Finance) successfully transfer across six distinct target domains (e.g., Code, Legal, Health, Edu), and key findings are corroborated across multiple architectures (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen-2.5-7B).

Exemplary analysis of limitations and failure modes: Rather than ignoring over-training failures, Section 5 systematically characterizes how emergent misalignment re-emerges under prolonged training, and methodically tests hypotheses (H1, H2, H3) via activation patching and layer-freezing experiments to localize upstream rerouting.
weaknesses: Small evaluation set size: The final evaluation benchmark consists of only 29 held-out prompts. While carefully curated from prior literature (Betley et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), expanding the evaluation suite would provide even stronger statistical confidence across diverse safety categories.

Dependency on an initial misaligned checkpoint: The latent discovery pipeline requires first fine-tuning an unconstrained misaligned model ($M^{\text{mis}}$) to conduct model diffing and causal screening. Although the authors demonstrate cross-domain transfer and release pre-discovered latents, this dependency limits out-of-the-box applicability to novel domains where misaligned behavior manifests through unknown representations.

Computational overhead during fine-tuning: Applying the BLOCK-EM loss requires forward passes through both the frozen base model and the SAE encoder at every training step, which introduces noticeable memory and compute overhead relative to standard supervised fine-tuning.

strengths: Principled integration of mechanistic interpretability and training-time defense: Rather than relying on blunt global penalties (such as KL divergence) or inference-time steering, the paper introduces a targeted, sign-aware one-sided latent blocking objective (BLOCK-EM) grounded in sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations.

Rigorous latent discovery and validation pipeline: The three-stage selection pipeline (activation shift, induce-and-repair causal screening, and calibrated ranking under an incoherence budget) is thoroughly ablated. Experiments clearly demonstrate that random latents fail, simple 'Top-Delta' shifts are insufficient, and signed directionality is critical.

Strong empirical results and cross-domain transfer: Demonstrates up to 93-95% reduction in emergent misalignment across six fine-tuning domains while maintaining high in-domain task adherence and low incoherence. Importantly, latents discovered on a single domain (Finance) successfully transfer across the remaining five domains.

High standard of scientific rigor in failure analysis: Rather than hiding the limitation that misalignment re-emerges under prolonged training, the authors systematically formulate and test three hypotheses (H1-H3) using downstream layer freezing, SAE reconstruction stability, and activation patching, localizing the rerouting effect to upstream representations.
weaknesses: Small evaluation prompt suites: The quantitative evaluation relies on 44 prompts for core discovery and 29 prompts for final evaluation. While derived from established benchmarks in recent literature, such small evaluation sets are susceptible to high variance and narrow behavioral coverage.

Dependency on an existing misaligned checkpoint for discovery: Applying BLOCK-EM to a new base model family requires first training a misaligned checkpoint ($M_{mis}$) and executing the three-stage screening pipeline. While the authors mitigate this for Llama-3.1-8B by releasing pre-computed latent sets, this upfront requirement adds friction for arbitrary new architectures.

Narrow scope of fine-tuning domains: All evaluated training domains consist of intentionally malicious or flawed objectives (e.g., bad financial advice, buggy code), following Wang et al. (2025). Evaluating whether the approach works when fine-tuning on standard benign domains that inadvertently cause emergent misalignment would further broaden the practical applicability.

Heuristic layer choice: Interventions are fixed at layer 20 (with a single ablation at layer 32). A more systematic exploration across multiple candidate intermediate layers would help establish guidelines for choosing optimal blocking layers.
